title: 論語 陽貨第十七
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 17, 〈陽貨〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 17 of the Analects, 陽貨 Yáng Huò, named, as every book is, from its first words — the name of Yang Huo, the retainer of the Ji house who had seized the government of Lu and wanted Confucius in his service. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 17 has 26 passages. It opens with Kongzi timing a courtesy call for when Yang Huo is out, and meeting him on the road anyway (17.1); then come two short sayings on human nature — people are born close together and grow apart by what they practise, and only the wisest and the most foolish are never moved (17.2–3). Twice a rebel sends for the Master and he is minded to go, and twice Zilu objects: the Master answers that what is truly hard is not worn thin, and he is no gourd to hang in one place uneaten (17.5, 17.7). There are the six good things that turn to faults without learning (17.8); a plea to the young to study the Odes (17.9); the man his village calls decent, who is the ruin of virtue (17.13); 'I have a mind to say nothing at all' — does Heaven speak? (17.19); Kongzi pleading illness to a caller and then singing so that he hears (17.20); and the long exchange with Zai Wo, who thinks three years of mourning for a parent too long (17.21). 17.17 repeats 1.3 word for word; He Yan's edition leaves it out. The book ends with the saying on the women and the servants of a household (17.25) and a man still disliked at forty (17.26). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

陽貨欲見孔子；
孔子不見。
歸孔子豚。
孔子時其亡也而往拜之；
遇諸塗。

sentences.i: Yang Huo wanted Kongzi to call on him, and Kongzi would not go. So Yang Huo had a young pig delivered to him. Kongzi picked a moment when Yang Huo was away from home and went to bow his thanks at his door — and ran into him on the road.
sentences.n: The book is named 陽貨 from its opening words; Zhu Xi counts twenty-six chapters (凡二十六章), and our numbers are his. 陽貨 Yang Huo, Zhu Xi says, was a retainer of the Ji house named Hu (陽貨季氏家臣名虎) — that is, Yang Hu, whom you met at 9.5, 16.2 and 16.3; he had once imprisoned Ji Huanzi and taken the government of the state into his own hands (嘗囚季桓子而專國政). He Yan's Kong Anguo agrees (陽貨陽虎也): a retainer of the Ji who ran the government of Lu and wanted to see Kongzi to make him take office. 見 jiàn 'to see' — Zhu Xi: he wanted to make Kongzi come and see him (欲令孔子來見己), and Kongzi would not go. 歸 here is 'to send as a gift'. Zhu Xi notes 歸如字一作饋: read it as written, guī, though one text writes 饋 'to present food' (those who follow 饋 read kuì). 豚 tún is a young pig. Zhu Xi explains the move: by the rites, when a grandee sent a gift to an officer and the officer could not receive it at his own house, he went and bowed at the grandee's gate (禮大夫有賜於士不得受於其家則往拜其門); so Huo watched for Kongzi to be out (瞰孔子之亡) and sent the pig, to make Kongzi come and bow and so meet him. 亡 is read wú, 'not there, away' (= 無). 時 is a verb here, 'to time it, to wait for the moment'. 諸 is the fused 之於 'him at': 遇諸塗 'met him on the road' (Kong Anguo: 塗道也). Zhu Xi weighs each step: not going to see him was what was right (義); going to bow was the rites (禮); choosing the time of his absence was to answer him in kind (欲其稱也); not avoiding him on the road was not cutting him off for ever (不終絶也).

sentences.l:
He said to Kongzi: “Come! I will talk with you.”
He said: “Holding one's treasure in one's bosom and leaving one's state astray — can that be called humane?”
He said: “It cannot.”
“Fond of taking part in affairs, and yet again and again missing the moment — can that be called wise?”
He said: “It cannot.”
“The days and months go by; the years do not stay for us.”
Kongzi said: “Very well. I am going to take office.”
sentences.i: He called out to Kongzi, “Come here, I have something to say to you. To hide away your treasure while your state goes astray — would you call that humane?” “No,” said Kongzi. “To long for a part in affairs and yet let the moment slip by time after time — would you call that wise?” “No.” “The days and months are slipping past, and the years will not linger for us.” “Very well,” said Kongzi. “In time I shall take office.”
sentences.n: 予 yú 'I'; 與 yǔ 'with'. 懷 is to hold in the bosom, to keep tucked away (15.6 可巻而懷之), 寶 bǎo a treasure, and 迷 mí 'lost, astray', here a verb with an object: to leave one's state in confusion. Zhu Xi: keeping the Way and virtue hidden and not saving the state from its confusion (懷寶迷邦謂懷藏道徳不救國之迷亂); He Yan's Ma Rong: not taking office is hiding the treasure, and knowing the state is ill governed yet not governing it is leaving it astray. 好 hào 'fond of'; 從事 'to take part in affairs'. 亟 qì 'often' (Zhu Xi: 亟數也), and 失時 is failing to be in time for the moment when things can be turned (失時謂不及事幾之㑹). 知 is zhì 'wise'. Zhu Xi marks 好亟知並去聲, all three as modern Mandarin reads them. He Yan's text writes 智 for 知 'wise', here and at 17.3 and 17.24 — the same word. 逝 shì 'to go by'; 嵗 is the edition's form of 歲 suì 'year'. 不我與 'not us stay-with': after a negative, a pronoun object comes before the verb (as 不己知, 1.16); 與 yǔ is to keep company with, to wait for. The text never names who answers 曰不可. Zhu Xi takes the answers as Kongzi's — he answered each question as it came because right was on his side (隨問而對者理之直也), and answered without arguing, his words yielding yet giving nothing away (對而不辯者言之孫而亦無所詘也). Huo's words, he says, all mocked Kongzi and hinted that he should take office quickly (貨語皆譏孔子而諷使速仕); Kongzi had never been as Huo described, nor was he unwilling to serve — only not under Huo (但不仕於貨耳), so he answered straight from principle as if he had missed the hint (若不諭其意者). 將 jiāng 'am going to': Zhu Xi, a word for what is about to be but is not yet certain (將者且然而未必之辭). Kong Anguo: with compliant words he kept out of harm. Zhu Xi adds that Huo's wish to see him, however kindly put, was only to get his help in disorder. He ends with Yang Shi: Yang Xiong said that with Yang Huo Kongzi 'paid respect where none was due, bending his person to make the Way prevail' (敬所不敬為詘身以信道) — a man who says this does not know Kongzi: there is no self outside the Way and no Way outside the self; bend the self, and can the Way be made to prevail? 'I do not believe it.'

sentences.t:
子曰：「
性相近也，
習相逺也。」

morph.gloss: by what they are steeped in

sentences.i: The Master said: “What people are born with keeps them close together; what they grow used to sets them far apart.”
sentences.n: Two clauses of one shape, each closed by 也, with no word to join them. 相 xiāng 'one another'; 逺 is the edition's form of 遠 yuǎn 'far'. 習 is the word of 1.1 'to rehearse', here what one is practised in until it becomes habit. Zhu Xi: the nature spoken of here includes the endowment of qi and substance (此所謂性兼氣質而言者也); natures so endowed certainly differ, finer and coarser, but taken at the start they are not far apart; practised in good one becomes good, practised in bad one becomes bad, and only then do they begin to be far apart (習於善則善習於惡則惡於是始相逺耳). He quotes Master Cheng: this speaks of the nature of qi and substance, not of the root of the nature; spoken of at its root, the nature simply is principle, and principle is never not good — Mencius' 'the nature is good' (孟子之言性善是也) — so how could there be any 'near'? He Yan's Kong Anguo draws the lesson: 君子慎所習也, the gentleman is careful what he practises.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
唯上知與下愚不移。」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Only the highest in wisdom and the lowest in folly do not shift.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Only the wisest of all and the most foolish of all are never moved from where they stand.”
sentences.n: 唯 wéi 'only'. 上知 'the highest wisdom' and 下愚 'the lowest folly' stand for the people who have them; 知 is zhì 'wisdom' (Zhu Xi: 知去聲), and 與 yǔ 'and' joins the pair. 移 yí 'to move, to shift'. Zhu Xi: this follows on from the chapter before — within the general nearness of endowment there are also the fine and the coarse, fixed once for all, which practice cannot shift (此承上章而言人之氣質相近之中又有美惡一定而非習之所能移者). He quotes Master Cheng: the human nature is good at root, so why are some unmovable? Speak of the nature, and all are good; speak of capacity, and there is the unmovable lowest folly. It is of two kinds, those who do violence to themselves and those who throw themselves away (自暴自棄也). Anyone who takes himself in hand with the good can be moved; even the dullest can be ground and polished and advance by degrees; but the one rejects the good by not believing, the other cuts it off by not acting, and even a sage living beside them could not change them. Such men need not be dull: often they are stubborn and fierce, with talents beyond others' — Xin of Shang (商辛) was one; the sage calls them the lowest folly because they cut themselves off from the good, and, looking at where they end, they are indeed foolish. Zhu Xi adds that some say this chapter belongs with the last, the 子曰 being an intrusion (或曰此與上章當合為一子曰二字盖衍文耳). He Yan's Kong Anguo: the highest wisdom cannot be forced to do evil, and the lowest folly cannot be forced to be worthy.

sentences.t:
子之武城，
聞絃歌之聲。
sentences.l:
The Master went to Wucheng
and heard the sound of strings and song.
sentences.i: The Master went to Wucheng, and there he heard zithers playing and voices raised in song.
sentences.n: 之 is a verb here, 'to go to' (as 5.18). 武城 Wucheng was a lesser town of Lu (6.12). 絃 xián is a string, here stringed instruments: Zhu Xi, 絃琴瑟也, the qin and se zithers. Zhu Xi: Ziyou was then steward of Wucheng (6.12) and made the rites and music his teaching, so the townspeople all played and sang (時子游為武城宰以禮樂為教故邑人皆絃歌也). He Yan's Kong Anguo also names Ziyou as steward.

sentences.t:
夫子莞爾而笑，曰：「
割雞焉用牛刀？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master smiled a small smile and said:
“To carve a chicken, why use the knife for an ox?”
sentences.i: The Master gave a faint smile. “Why take a blade meant for oxen to a chicken?” he said.
sentences.n: 夫子 fū zǐ is the Master as the disciples speak of him. 莞爾 is 'with a small smile': Zhu Xi, 莞爾小笑貌, and He Yan's comment has the same words; 爾 makes a description of manner, as in 率爾 (11.25). Zhu Xi spells 莞 華版反, which points to huǎn; we give the modern reading wǎn. 而 joins the manner to the verb. 焉 yān 'how, why' (Zhu Xi: 於䖍反). 雞 jī a chicken, 刀 dāo a knife. Zhu Xi: he was pleased (盖喜之也), and so said that in governing a small town there was no need for so great a Way (因言其治小邑何必用此大道也). He Yan's Kong Anguo reads the jest the same way.

sentences.t:
子游對曰：「
昔者偃也聞諸夫子曰：『
君子學道則愛人；
小人學道則易使也。』」

sentences.l:
Ziyou answered:
“Once I, Yan, heard it from you, Master:
‘When the gentleman learns the Way, he loves others;
when the small man learns the Way, he is easy to employ.’”
sentences.i: Ziyou answered, “Master, I once heard you say: ‘When those in high place learn the Way, they love others; when the common people learn the Way, they are easy to set to work.’”
sentences.n: 子游 Ziyou is Yan Yan 言偃 (2.7), who names himself 偃 'Yan' to his teacher (6.12). 昔者 'in former days'. 諸 is the fused 之於: 聞諸夫子 'heard it from you, Master'. 則 'then' joins each condition to its result. 道 dào 'the Way'; 易 yì 'easy' (Zhu Xi: 易去聲, as modern Mandarin reads it); 使 shǐ 'to employ, to direct'. Zhu Xi: here 君子 and 小人 are spoken of by rank, not by character (君子小人以位言之) — those who govern and those who are governed; what Ziyou quotes was probably the Master's regular saying (盖夫子之常言), that high and low alike must learn, so even a town as small as Wucheng must be taught the rites and music. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 道禮樂也樂以和人人和則易使也 — the Way is the rites and music; music brings people to ease, and people at ease are easy to direct. He Yan's text ends 則易使, without the final 也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
二三子！
偃之言是也；
前言戲之耳。」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“My friends!
Yan's words are right;
my words before were only teasing him.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “My friends, Yan has it right. I was only having some fun with him just now.”
sentences.n: 二三子 'my friends' is the Master addressing the disciples with him (3.24); He Yan's Kong Anguo: those travelling with him (從行者也). 是 here is 'right' — the opposite of 非 'wrong' — not 'this'. 前言 'the earlier words'. 戲 xì 'to tease, to joke'; 之 'him'; 耳 at the end is 'only, and that is all'. Zhu Xi: he was praising Ziyou's firm faith and clearing up the disciples' puzzlement (嘉子游之篤信又以觧門人之惑也). Governing may be on a large scale or a small one, but that it must use the rites and music makes it one Way; most people cannot use it and Ziyou alone put it into practice, so the Master, coming on it unexpectedly, was deeply pleased, turned his own words round to tease him, and when Ziyou answered him straight, affirmed what he said and owned that he had been joking (故復是其言而自實其戲也). Kong Anguo: the joke was about using the great Way to govern a small place.

sentences.t:
公山弗擾以費畔，
召，
子欲往。

words.reading: 公山弗擾 gōng shān fú rǎo

sentences.i: Gongshan Furao held the town of Bi in revolt and sent for the Master, and the Master was minded to go.
sentences.n: 公山弗擾 Gongshan Furao: Gongshan is the surname, Furao the personal name. Zhu Xi: he was a steward of the Ji (弗擾季氏宰), who with Yang Hu (17.1) seized Ji Huanzi and held his town in revolt (據邑以叛). He Yan's Kong Anguo tells the same story (不擾為季氏宰與陽虎共執季桓子而召孔子也). 費 bì is Bi, the Ji's walled town (6.7, 11.24, 16.1). 以 'with, by means of' — holding Bi; 畔 pàn 'to rebel' (= 叛). 召 zhào 'to summon'; the one summoned is understood. 欲往 'wanted to go': the text does not say he went. Variant: He Yan's text writes the name 公山不擾, with 不 for 弗 — the same man.

sentences.t:
子路不説，曰：「
末之也已，
何必公山氏之之也？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zilu was not pleased. “If there is nowhere to go, then there is nowhere,” he said. “Why must you go to Gongshan, of all people?”
sentences.n: 説 is yuè 'pleased' (Zhu Xi: 説音悦). 末 mò is 'there is none' (Zhu Xi: 末無也), and 之 here is the verb 'to go' (He Yan's Kong Anguo: 之適也); 也已 closes the clause, 'and that is that'. Zhu Xi: the Way not being put into practice, there is nowhere to go — but why must it be to Gongshan that you go? (言道既不行無所往矣何必公山氏之往乎). Kong Anguo: with nowhere one may go, one stops, that is all (無可之則止耳). 公山氏 'the Gongshan man', 氏 after a surname. In 公山氏之之 the object comes first: the first 之 marks it as put before its verb, and the second 之 is the verb 'to go to' — 'why must it be Gongshan that you go to?' Variant: He Yan's text reads 未之也巳, 未 'not yet' for 末 — probably a slip, since Kong Anguo's own reading is 'nowhere to go'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
夫召我者而豈徒哉？
如有用我者，
吾其為東周乎！」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Now, the one who summons me — how could it be for nothing?
If there were one who would use me,
would I not make a Zhou in the east?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The man who sends for me — would he do so for nothing? If anyone would put me to use, might I not raise up the Way of Zhou once more, here in the east?”
sentences.n: 夫 fú opens the topic, 'now' (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶). 召我者 'the one who summons me'; 而 stands between the topic and the question and needs no word in English. 豈…哉 'how could it be…?' asks a question that expects 'no'; 徒 'for nothing'. Zhu Xi: 豈徒哉 means he will surely use me (言必用我也). 吾其…乎 'would I not…?': 其 softens and strengthens at once, 'surely'. 為 wéi 'to make'. 東周 is not here the name of a period: Zhu Xi reads 為東周 as raising up the Way of Zhou in the east (興周道於東方), and He Yan's comment says the same. He quotes Master Cheng: the sage held that in the world there is no man with whom nothing can be done, and none who cannot correct his faults, so he wanted to go; that in the end he did not go was because he knew this man could certainly not change (然而終不往者知其必不能改故也).

sentences.t:
子張問仁於孔子。
孔子曰：「能行五者於天下，為仁矣。」「
請問之。」
曰：「恭、寛、信、敏、惠。
恭則不侮；
寛則得衆；
信則人任焉；
敏則有功；
惠則足以使人。」

sentences.i: Zizhang asked Kongzi about humaneness. Kongzi said: “Whoever can put five things into practice wherever he goes under Heaven is humane.” “May I ask what they are?” “Respect, breadth of mind, good faith, quickness and kindness. Show respect, and no one treats you with contempt; be broad-minded, and the many come over to you; keep your word, and people put their weight on you; be quick, and things get done; be kind, and you have what it takes to set others to work.”
sentences.n: 子張 Zizhang is Zhuansun Shi 顓孫師 (2.18). 問仁於孔子 'asked about humaneness of Kongzi': 於 marks the man asked. 行 xíng 'to put into practice'; 五者 'five things'; 為 wéi 'is, counts as'. 於天下, Zhu Xi says, means wherever one goes it holds (於天下言無適而不然), like 'even among the Yi and Di, not to be cast aside' (13.19). Zizhang's 請問之 has no 曰; the speaker is understood. 寛 is the edition's form of 寬 'broad-minded'. 侮 'to slight' (He Yan's Kong Anguo: not to be treated with contempt, 不見侮慢也). 任 rèn 'to lean on, rely on' (Zhu Xi: 任倚仗也), with 焉 yān 'on him'. 敏 'quick' — Kong Anguo: meeting affairs promptly, one accomplishes much. 足以 'enough to'; 使 shǐ 'to employ'. Zhu Xi: practise these five and the mind is kept and principle grasped (行是五者則心存而理得矣); and the five were named for what Zizhang lacked (葢因子張所不足而言耳). He quotes Zhang Jingfu (Zhang Shi): one who can practise them everywhere has a mind fair and all-embracing; yet respect is perhaps the root (然恭其本與). And a Mr Li (李氏): this chapter, like the 'six words and six cloudings' (17.8) and the 'five excellences and four evils' (五美四惡) in a later book, is quite unlike the style of the text around it. Variant: He Yan's text reads 孔子對曰, 'Kongzi answered'.

sentences.t:
佛肸召，
子欲往。
sentences.l:
Bi Xi summoned (the Master),
and the Master wanted to go.
sentences.i: Bi Xi sent for the Master, and the Master was minded to go.
sentences.n: 佛肸 Bi Xi: Zhu Xi gives the readings, 佛音弼 — 佛 is read bì, like 弼 — and 肸許密反, which we give in its modern form xī. He was, Zhu Xi says, steward of Zhongmou for the Zhao, a grandee house of Jin (佛肸晉大夫趙氏之中牟宰也); He Yan's Kong Anguo: steward of a town of Zhao Jianzi, a grandee of Jin (晉大夫趙簡子之邑宰). 召 zhào 'to summon'. The chapter is built like 17.5.

子路曰：「昔者由也聞諸夫子曰：『
親於其身為不善者，
君子不入也。』
佛肸以中牟畔；
子之往也，如之何？」

sentences.l:
Zilu said: “Once I, Yóu, heard it from you, Master:
‘One who in his own person does what is not good —
the gentleman does not go in among them.’
Bi Xi holds Zhongmou in revolt;
your going there — how is that?”
sentences.i: Zilu said: “Master, I once heard you say that a gentleman will not join a man who himself does wrong. Now Bi Xi has raised Zhongmou in revolt — how can you think of going?”
sentences.n: 由 Yóu is Zilu's personal name; he names himself by it, as Ziyou names himself 偃 in 17.4. 昔者 'once, in former days'; 諸 the fused 之於, 'it from'. Zhu Xi: 親猶自也, 親 is 'oneself, in one's own person'; and 不入 is not entering his party (不入其黨也) — He Yan's own comment says 'his state' (不入其國). 為 wéi 'to do'. 中牟 zhōng móu Zhongmou is the town Bi Xi kept for the Zhao. 子之往也 'your going': 之 between subject and verb turns the clause into a noun, 'as for your going'. 如之何 'how is that?' (2.20). Zhu Xi: Zilu feared that Bi Xi would soil the Master (子路恐佛肸之浼夫子), and asked this to stop him from going. Variant: He Yan's text reads 君子不入, without 也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「然，有是言也。
不曰堅乎？磨而不磷；
不曰白乎？涅而不緇。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Yes, there are those words.
Do we not say ‘hard’? Ground, and not worn thin.
Do we not say ‘white’? Soaked in black dye-earth, and not darkened.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Yes, I did say that. But don't we also speak of a thing so hard that no grinding wears it thin, and of a thing so white that soaking it in dye cannot darken it?”
sentences.n: 然 'so it is'; 是言 'these words'. 不曰…乎 'do we not say…?' brings in common words to answer common words. 磨 'to grind'; 磷 lìn 'thin' (Zhu Xi: 磷力刃反…磷薄也; Kong Anguo the same). 涅 niè (Zhu Xi: 乃結反) is a stuff for dyeing black (涅染皁物), used here as a verb; 緇 zī 'black', here 'to go black'. Zhu Xi: others' wrongdoing cannot soil him. He Yan's Kong Anguo: the hardest thing, ground, does not thin; the whitest, dyed with 涅, does not blacken; so the gentleman, though he live amid filth and disorder, cannot be stained by it (君子雖在濁亂濁亂不能汚也). Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi as a warning: only one whom grinding does not thin and dye does not blacken can be free of 'may' and 'may not' (無可無不可); one whose hardness and whiteness are not enough, who wants to test himself against grinding and dyeing, will seldom come through unthinned and unblackened (其不磷緇也者幾希). Variant: He Yan's text reads 然有是言曰, 曰 for 也 — probably a slip.

sentences.t:
吾豈匏瓜也哉？
焉能繫而不食？
sentences.l:
Am I a gourd, then?
How could I hang tied in one place and not eat?
sentences.i: Am I a gourd on a string, to hang in one spot and never feed?
sentences.n: The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment and are left unquoted. 豈…哉 'how could I…!' — a question that expects 'no'. 匏 páo is a gourd (Zhu Xi, and He Yan's own comment: 匏瓠也); 繫 xì 'to tie, to hang'. 焉 yān 'how' (Zhu Xi: 於䖍反). 食 shí 'to eat'. Taken alone, 繫而不食 could also mean 'hung up and not eaten'; both commentaries read 'not eat'. Zhu Xi: a gourd hangs fixed in one place and cannot drink or eat, and a man is not like that (匏瓜繫於一處而不能飲食人則不如是也). He Yan's own comment: the gourd can be hung in one place because it does not eat; 'I am a thing that eats, and must go east, west, south and north; I cannot be like a thing that does not eat, hung fixed in one place.' Zhu Xi ends with Zhang Jingfu (Zhang Shi): what Zilu had heard was the gentleman's constant rule for keeping himself; what the Master says now is the great discretion of a sage who embodies the Way (聖人體道之大權也). He wanted to go at both summonses, Gongshan's and Bi Xi's, because there is no man in the world who cannot be changed and no task that cannot be done; that in the end he did not go was because he knew those men would never change and the task could never be done — the one is the humaneness that gives life to things, the other the wisdom that knows men (一則生物之仁一則知人之智也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
由也！
女聞六言六蔽矣乎？」
對曰：「未也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Yóu!
Have you heard the six words and the six cloudings?”
He answered: “Not yet.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Yóu, have you heard of the six words, and the six ways each of them can be clouded over?” “Not yet,” Zilu answered.
sentences.n: 由 Yóu is Zilu, called by his personal name; 也 after it sets the name off. 女 is rǔ 'you' (Zhu Xi: 女音汝下同). 六言 'the six words' are six good qualities, a word each; He Yan's comment lists them as the six matters that follow — humaneness, wisdom, good faith, straightness, courage, firmness (六言六蔽下六事謂仁智信直勇剛也). 蔽 bì is a covering over: Zhu Xi, 蔽遮掩也, 'to screen, to hide from view' — the fault that comes over each virtue and hides it. 矣乎 together: 矣 for a state already reached, 乎 the question — 'have you heard them yet?' 對 'answered', to a superior.

sentences.t:
居！
吾語女。
sentences.l:
Sit!
I will tell you.
sentences.i: Sit down again, and I will tell you.
sentences.n: The Master's words, left unquoted after Zhu Xi's comment. 居 is 'sit', 'be seated'. 語 is yù 'to tell' (Zhu Xi: 語去聲); 女 rǔ 'you'. Zhu Xi explains the order: by the rites, when the gentleman one is with asks about a new matter, one rises to answer (禮君子問更端則起而對), so Kongzi had Zilu go back to his seat and then told him (使還坐而告之). He Yan's Kong Anguo: 子路起對故使還坐也, Zilu had risen to answer, so the Master had him sit down again.

sentences.t:
好仁不好學，其蔽也愚；
好知不好學，其蔽也蕩；
好信不好學，其蔽也賊；
好直不好學，其蔽也絞；
好勇不好學，其蔽也亂；
好剛不好學，其蔽也狂。
sentences.i: Love humaneness but not learning, and it clouds over into folly. Love wisdom but not learning, and it clouds over into aimless drifting. Love good faith but not learning, and it clouds over into doing harm. Love straightness but not learning, and it clouds over into harshness. Love courage but not learning, and it clouds over into unruliness. Love firmness but not learning, and it clouds over into recklessness.
sentences.n: Six lines of one shape, still the Master speaking. 好 is hào 'to be fond of' all twelve times, and 知 is zhì 'wisdom' (Zhu Xi: 好知並去聲). 其蔽也愚 'its clouding is folly': 其 'its', of the quality loved; 也 pauses after the topic. Zhu Xi: the six words are all fine virtues, but to love them merely, without learning to make their principle clear, is to have each clouded (六言皆美徳然徒好之而不學以明其理則各有所蔽). He glosses: 愚 is the kind of folly that can be trapped and fooled (愚若可陷可罔之類 — the words of 6.24); 蕩 is reaching for the highest and widest with nowhere to stop (蕩謂窮髙極廣而無所止); 賊 is doing harm to things (賊謂傷害於物); courage is firmness put forth, and firmness the body of courage (勇者剛之發剛者勇之體); 狂 is rash and headlong (狂躁率也). 絞 is 'harsh, cutting' as in 8.2 (直而無禮則絞), where 亂 follows courage too (勇而無禮則亂; cf. 8.10). He Yan's Kong Anguo: the humane love things but do not know how to cut that love to measure, and so are foolish (仁者愛物不知所以裁之則愚); 蕩 is drifting with no mean to hold to (蕩無所適中也); 賊 is father and son who do not know to cover for each other (父子不知相爲隱之輩; compare 13.18); 狂 is wild, butting against others (狂妄抵觸人). Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: Zilu was brave in doing good, but where he failed was in not yet loving learning to make it clear, so he was told this; and courage, firmness, good faith and straightness were each named to correct his one-sidedness (又皆所以救其偏也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
小子！
何莫學夫詩？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Young men!
Why does none of you learn those Odes?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Young men, why do you leave the Odes unlearned, every one of you?”
sentences.n: 小子 'young men' — Zhu Xi: 小子弟子也, the disciples; He Yan's Bao Xian: 小子門人也. 何莫 'why does no one': 莫 'none'. 夫 fú 'those', pointing at the Odes (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶). 詩 is the Odes (1.15). Zhu Xi stops after each of the clauses that follow to gloss it in a few words; the Master's speech runs on through them and is left unquoted there.

sentences.t: 詩可以興，
sentences.l: The Odes can stir you,
sentences.i: The Odes can rouse you;
sentences.n: 可以 'can be used to'. 興 xīng 'to rise, to be roused', as in 8.8 興於詩. Zhu Xi: 感發志意, they move and rouse the will. He Yan's Kong Anguo takes it as the poet's figure: 興引譬連類, 'xing is drawing on comparisons and linking things of a kind'.

sentences.t: 可以觀，
sentences.l: can let you observe,
sentences.i: they can teach you to look and judge;
sentences.n: 觀 'to observe'. Zhu Xi: 考見得失, to examine and see what succeeds and what fails. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: to observe the rise and decline of customs (觀風俗之盛衰).

sentences.t: 可以羣，
sentences.l: can let you keep company,
sentences.i: they can help you live among others;
sentences.n: 羣 is the edition's form of 群 qún: a flock, and as a verb to keep company with others (15.21). Zhu Xi: 和而不流, at ease with others without being carried along by them. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 羣居相切磋也, living in company and cutting and polishing one another (the 切磋 of 1.15).

sentences.t: 可以怨；
sentences.l: can let you voice grievance;
sentences.i: they can give a voice to grievance.
sentences.n: 怨 'to resent, to complain'. Zhu Xi: 怨而不怒, to complain without anger. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 怨刺上政, to complain of and prick at the government above.

sentences.t:
邇之事父，
逺之事君；
sentences.l:
Near at hand, with them you serve your father;
far off, you serve your lord;
sentences.i: Close to home they teach you to serve your father, and further afield to serve your lord;
sentences.n: 邇 ěr 'near' (He Yan's Kong Anguo: 邇近也); 逺 yuǎn 'far' (the edition's form of 遠). 之 after each is hard to pin down: either 'them', the Odes put to use, or a light word that makes 'near' and 'far' into adverbs; the sense comes out the same. 事 'to serve'. Zhu Xi: the Odes lack nothing of the way of human bonds; these two are named as the weightiest (人倫之道詩無不備二者舉重而言).

sentences.t: 多識於鳥獸草木之名。
sentences.l: and you come to know much of the names of birds and beasts, grasses and trees.
sentences.i: and from them you learn the names of a great many birds and beasts, grasses and trees.
sentences.n: 識 is read shí here, 'to come to know, to recognize'; Zhu Xi gives it no mark. 獸 shòu 'a beast'. 於 'about, of'. Zhu Xi: even the loose ends of the Odes are enough to furnish wide knowledge (其緒餘又足以資多識). He closes the chapter: the method of learning the Odes is told in full here, and those who read this classic should give their whole mind to it (學詩之法此章盡之讀是經者所宜盡心也).

sentences.t:
子謂伯魚曰：「
女為《周南》、《召南》矣乎？
人而不為《周南》、《召南》，
其猶正牆面而立也與？」

morph.gloss: fish (魚餒而肉敗 'when the fish is rotten and the meat spoiled')

sentences.l:
The Master said to Bo Yu:
“Have you studied the Zhounan and the Shaonan?
A man who has not studied the Zhounan and the Shaonan —
is he not like one standing with his face squarely to a wall?”
sentences.i: The Master said to Bo Yu: “Have you worked through the Zhounan and the Shaonan yet? A man who has not is like someone standing with his nose to a wall.”
sentences.n: 伯魚 Bo Yu is Kong Li, the Master's son (16.13). 女 is rǔ 'you' (Zhu Xi: 女音汝). 為 wéi here is 'to study': Zhu Xi: 為 is like 學 (為猶學也). 周南 and 召南 (召 read shào) are the first two sections of the Airs of the States in the Odes; the Guanju of 3.20 is the first poem of the Zhounan. Zhu Xi: they are names of the opening sections of the Odes, and what they speak of is all the business of cultivating oneself and ordering one's household (周南召南詩首篇名所言皆修身齊家之事). Ma Rong in He Yan: they are the beginning of the Airs of the States (國風之始) — a good maiden matched with a gentleman, the head of the three bonds and the starting point of the royal teaching — so a man who does not study them is like one facing a wall. 矣乎 'by now…?'. 人而不為 'a man, and yet not studying' (the shape of 3.3 人而不仁). 其猶…也與 'is he not like…?', with 與 yú closing the question (Zhu Xi: 與平聲). 正牆面而立 'standing with his face squarely to a wall': Zhu Xi: it means that in the very nearest place he sees not one thing and cannot take a single step (即其至近之地而一物無所見一步不可行).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
禮云禮云，
玉帛云乎哉？
樂云樂云，
鐘鼓云乎哉？」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“‘The rites,’ they say, ‘the rites’ —
is it jade and silk they are speaking of?
‘Music,’ they say, ‘music’ —
is it bells and drums they are speaking of?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “People speak of the rites, the rites — is it jade and silk they have in mind? They speak of music, music — is it bells and drums they have in mind?”
sentences.n: 云 is 'to say', and the word said twice over is the word men have always on their lips. 乎哉 joins a question to an exclamation: 'is it… that is meant?', expecting no. 玉帛 'jade and silk', the gifts presented in ceremony; 鐘鼓 'bells and drums'; 樂 is yuè 'music' throughout. Zhu Xi: offered with reverence and presented with jade and silk, it is the rites; set going with ease and sounded out on bells and drums, it is music; to leave the root and attend only to the branches — how could that be called rites and music (遺其本而專事其末則豈禮樂之謂哉)? He quotes Master Cheng: the rites are simply order (序), music simply ease (和), and these two words hold a great deal of principle; nothing in the world is without rites and music: set two chairs here, one of them not straight, and there is no order, and without order there is discord, and discord is not ease; even robbers, the most lawless of men, have rites and music, for they must have someone over them and heed one another, or they could not stay together a single day to rob. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: jade means tablets of jade (珪璋之屬), silk the bundled silk of gifts (束帛之屬); what the rites value is not these, but setting superiors at peace and governing the people (安上治民); Ma Rong: what music values is changing manners and customs (移風易俗), not bells and drums alone.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
色厲而内荏，
譬諸小人，
其猶穿窬之盗也與？」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Stern in look and soft within —
to liken him to one among the small folk,
is he not like a thief who bores through walls and climbs over them?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man with a stern face and nothing firm inside — look for his like among the common people, and you find the burglar who tunnels through a wall or slips over it.”
sentences.n: 色 'the look of the face'; 厲 'stern' (Zhu Xi: 厲威嚴也); 内 is the edition's form of 內 'within'; 荏 rěn (Zhu Xi: 而審反) 'soft and weak' (荏柔弱也). 譬諸 'to liken him to (one) among': 諸 is the fused 之於. 小人 here is not the small man of character: Zhu Xi: 小人 are the small folk, the common people (小人細民也). 穿 chuān is boring through a wall, 窬 yú climbing over one (Zhu Xi: 穿穿壁窬踰牆); 之 makes 穿窬 describe the thief; 盗 is the edition's form of 盜. 也與, with 與 yú (Zhu Xi: 與平聲), asks 'is he not…?'. Zhu Xi: it means he has no substance, steals a name, and is always afraid of being found out (言其無實盗名而常畏人知也). Kong Anguo in He Yan: 荏 is 'soft'; outwardly he makes himself proud and stern, inwardly he is soft and glib (外自矝厲而内柔佞); a man like that is like a petty man with a thief's heart.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
鄉原，徳之賊也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“The village paragon is the despoiler of virtue.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The man his village holds up as a model of decency is the ruin of virtue.”
sentences.n: 鄉原 is a type, and Zhu Xi explains both words: 鄉 has the sense of rustic, common (鄉者鄙俗之意), and 原 is the same as 愿 'honest, scrupulous' (原與愿同), as in Xunzi's 原慤, which the commentary on Xunzi reads as 愿 (荀子原慤註讀作愿是也); so the 鄉原 is the one among the villagers counted honest (鄉原鄉人之愿者也). We read xiāng yuàn, as the word 愿; Zhu Xi gives no sound mark. 徳 is the edition's form of 德; 賊 'despoiler' (as 14.46). Zhu Xi: he goes along with the current and joins in the muck to please the world (同流合汙以媚於世), so among the villagers he alone is called honest; because he seems virtuous and is not, and so confounds virtue, the Master called him its despoiler and hated him deeply; for more, see the last book of Mencius (詳見孟子末篇). He Yan's Zhou Shenglie reads 原 otherwise, as a verb: wherever he goes he gauges people's feelings and shapes his own mind to treat them accordingly, and that despoils virtue; and he gives a second explanation, taking 鄉 as 向 'to face toward' (the old graph being the same): a man who cannot be firm and, on meeting people, at once gauges which way they lean and fawns to fit them.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
道聽而塗説，
徳之棄也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Hearing on the road and telling along the way —
that is virtue abandoned.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “To pick something up on the road and pass it straight on to the next man you meet is to let virtue go to waste.”
sentences.n: 道 dào and 塗 tú (= 途) are both 'road', and the two halves make one picture: what is heard in the road is told again further down it. 説 is shuō 'to tell'. 徳之棄 'virtue's casting off' — 之 makes it a phrase: virtue thrown away. Zhu Xi: though he hears good words, he does not make them his own, and so throws away his own virtue (雖聞善言不為己有是自棄其徳也). He quotes Mr Wang (王氏): the gentleman learns much of the words and deeds of the past to store up his virtue; to hear on the road and tell on the way is to throw it away. Ma Rong in He Yan: he hears it on the road and at once passes it on (聞之於道路則傳而說之). Variant: He Yan's text reads 德之棄, without 也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
鄙夫可與事君也與哉？」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“A mean fellow — can one serve a lord alongside him?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “How could anyone serve a lord in company with a mean-spirited man?”
sentences.n: 鄙夫 'a mean fellow': Zhu Xi: a name for one who is commonplace, bad, low and base (鄙夫庸惡陋劣之稱); 夫 is fū 'a man'. 可與 'can one, with him' — 與 yǔ 'with'. 也與哉 piles a question on an exclamation, and the answer expected is no; the second 與 is yú (Zhu Xi: 與平聲). Kong Anguo in He Yan: it means one cannot serve a lord with him (言不可與事君). The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next two units are left unquoted. Variant: He Yan's text reads 鄙夫可與事君哉, without 也與.

sentences.t:
其未得之也，患得之；
既得之，患失之。
sentences.l:
Before he has got it, he frets about getting it;
once he has got it, he frets about losing it.
sentences.i: Before he has it, his one worry is how to get it; once he has it, his one worry is that he may lose it.
sentences.n: Still the Master, unquoted. 之 'it' is never named: the rank and wealth such a man is after, as Hu Yin's comment on the next unit makes plain. 其…也 sets the time: 'he, when he has not yet got it'. 既 'once, already'. 患 'to be troubled about'. 患得之 is a compressed way of saying 'frets about (not) getting it': Zhu Xi quotes Mr He (何氏): 'fretting about getting it' means fretting about not being able to get it (患得之謂患不能得之) — the words are He Yan's own comment, which adds that this is a Chu way of speaking (楚俗言). Variants: Ruan Yuan's text spells it out, 患不得之 'frets that he will not get it'; He Yan's text reads 其未得之患得之, without 也.

sentences.t:
苟患失之，
無所不至矣。
sentences.l:
If he frets about losing it,
there is nothing he will not go to.
sentences.i: And a man afraid of losing it — there is no depth he will not sink to.
sentences.n: Still the Master, unquoted. 苟 'if'. 無所不至 'there is nothing he does not reach': 所 makes 'what he does not go to' a noun, and 無 denies there is any. Zhu Xi: in small things, sucking abscesses and licking piles; in great things, murdering his father and his lord — all born of fretting about loss (小則吮癰舐痔大則弑父與君皆生於患失而已). He quotes Hu Yin, citing Jin Caizhi of Xuchang: scholars come in roughly three grades — those set on the Way and virtue, whose hearts fame and achievement cannot weigh down; those set on fame and achievement, whose hearts wealth and rank cannot weigh down; and those set on wealth and rank and nothing else, who will go to any length; the last are what Kongzi calls the mean fellow. Zheng Xuan in He Yan: 'nothing he will not go to' means there is no wicked fawning he will not do (言邪媚無所不為也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 苟患失無所不至矣, without 之.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
古者民有三疾，
今也或是之亡也。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “The people of old had three failings; today, it may be, they do not even have those.”
sentences.n: 古者 'in old times'. 疾 'sickness', here a failing of temperament: Zhu Xi: when one's vital breath (氣) loses its balance it is sickness, so a lopsided endowment is also called a sickness (氣失其平則為疾故氣稟之偏者亦謂之疾). 或 'perhaps'. 是之亡 'these, (they) lack': the object 是 'these' is put before the verb, and 之 marks it; 亡 is wú, = 無 'to lack' (as 3.5, 6.2). Zhu Xi: what were once called failings, now even they are gone — grieving that customs have declined still further (傷俗之益衰也). Bao Xian in He Yan: the people's failings in antiquity differed from those of the present day. The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next unit is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
古之狂也肆，
今之狂也蕩；
古之矜也廉，
今之矜也忿戾；
古之愚也直，
今之愚也詐而已矣。
sentences.i: In the old days the wild ones were careless of small proprieties; today's wild ones break through every bound. The stiff-necked of old were all sharp corners; today's are merely bad-tempered and perverse. The simple of old were at least straightforward; today's simple ones are nothing but cunning.
sentences.n: Still the Master, unquoted: six clauses of one shape, 'X's Y 也 Z', setting each failing of old beside what it has become. 狂 'the wild' (as 5.21, 13.21); 矜 here is a failing, not the gravity of 15.21; 愚 'the simple, the dull'. Zhu Xi: the wild have aims and wishes too high; 肆 is not being held by small proprieties (不拘小節); 蕩 is overstepping the great barriers (踰大閑); the stiff hold to themselves too strictly (矜者持守太嚴); 廉 is having sharp corners and edges (稜角陗厲); 忿戾 goes as far as quarrelling (忿戾則至於爭矣); the simple are dim and not clear-sighted; 直 is going straight ahead and doing as they please (徑行自遂); 詐 is harbouring private ends and acting wildly (挾私妄作). 廉 lián; 戾 lì. 而已矣 'and that is all'. He quotes Fan Zuyu: in a late age falsehood multiplies; it is not only that the worthy fall short of the ancients — the very faults of the people's nature differ from those of the men of old. He Yan's commentators: Bao Xian, 肆 is going to the limit of one's meaning and daring to speak (肆極意敢言); Kong Anguo, 蕩 is having nothing to hold to (蕩無所據); Ma Rong, 廉 is having edges and corners (有㢘隅也); Kong Anguo, 忿戾 is hating reason and being much given to anger (悪理多怒).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
巧言令色，
鮮矣仁！」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Clever words, a pleasing face —
rare indeed, humaneness!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Smooth talk and a face put on to please: seldom is there humaneness in them.”
sentences.n: The same words as 1.3, and the same English; see the note there. Zhu Xi's whole comment here is 重出 'appears a second time'. He Yan's text does not have the chapter in this book at all; Ruan Yuan's text has it, as Zhu Xi does.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
惡紫之奪朱也，
惡鄭聲之亂雅樂也，
惡利口之覆邦家者。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “I hate to see purple win out over vermilion, the sounds of Zheng muddle the proper music, and glib tongues bring states and great houses to ruin.”
sentences.n: 惡 is wù 'to hate' (Zhu Xi: 惡去聲), three times over. In each clause 之 turns what follows the verb into one phrase, 'purple's robbing vermilion'; the third clause ends in 者 'the ones that…'. Zhu Xi: vermilion is a true colour, purple a 'between' colour (朱正色紫閒色; see 10.6); 雅 is 'correct' (雅正也); 利口 is being quick and ready of tongue (捷給); 覆 fù (芳服反) is 'to topple, to bring down' (傾敗也). 鄭聲 'the sounds of Zheng', as 15.10; 樂 is yuè. He quotes Fan Zuyu: in the world, what is right and wins is ever rare, what is not right and wins ever common, and that is why the sage hates it; the man of sharp tongue makes right wrong and wrong right, the worthy unworthy and the unworthy worthy; if a ruler is pleased with him and believes him, the overturning of his state is not hard. He Yan's Kong Anguo: vermilion is a true colour, purple the most attractive of the between colours; he hates its wrong attractiveness taking the place of the true colour (悪其邪好而奪正色); the man of sharp tongue talks much and has little substance, and if he can please the ruler of the day he overturns his state; Bao Xian: the sounds of Zheng are wanton sounds, of the mournful kind, and he hates their taking the place of the proper music. Variant: He Yan's text has neither 也 and no final 者 (惡紫之奪朱，惡鄭聲之亂雅樂，惡利口之覆邦家).

sentences.t: 子曰：「予欲無言。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “I would like to have no words.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I have a mind to say nothing at all.”
sentences.n: 予 is yú 'I'. 欲 'to wish'; 無言 'to be without words, not to speak'. Zhu Xi: learners mostly look at the sage through his words, and do not perceive the reality of Heaven's principle flowing and moving, which is plain without waiting for words; so they get his words only, and not that from which he speaks; therefore the Master said this to rouse them (故夫子發此以警之). He Yan's comment, set after Zigong's reply: speaking does little good, so he wished to say nothing (言之為益少故欲無言也).

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
子如不言，
則小子何述焉？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said:
“Master, if you do not speak,
then what are we young ones to hand on?”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “If you say nothing, sir, what will we your students have to pass on?”
sentences.n: 子 here is 'you, Master', Zigong speaking to him. 如 'if'. 小子 'we young ones', the disciples naming themselves (as a master calls his disciples in 5.21 and 8.3). 述 'to hand on' — the word of 7.1 述而不作. 何述 'what hand on': the question word goes before the verb. 焉 yān closes the question. Zhu Xi: Zigong was just one who looked at the sage through his words, so he doubted and asked (子貢正以言語觀聖人者故疑而問之).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
天何言哉？
四時行焉，
百物生焉，
天何言哉？」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“What words has Heaven?
The four seasons move on there,
the hundred things are born there.
What words has Heaven?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Does Heaven make speeches? Yet the seasons follow one another, and all that lives comes to birth. Does Heaven make speeches?”
sentences.n: 天何言哉 'Heaven — what does it say?': the question word goes before the verb, and 哉 turns the question into an exclamation that expects 'nothing'. 四時 'the four seasons'; 行 xíng 'to go, to move on'; 百物 'the hundred things', every creature (物 wù); 生 'to be born, to grow'. 焉 yān closes each clause; it can be read as 'there, in it' (= 於之) or as a plain final particle. Zhu Xi: the seasons moving and the hundred things growing are nothing but the reality of Heaven's principle showing itself and flowing — it can be seen without waiting for words; the sage's every movement and rest is likewise nothing but the issuing of the subtle Way and its fine meaning (妙道精義之發), and he too is simply Heaven — why wait for words to make it plain? This, too, was a pointed showing to Zigong; a pity that in the end he did not understand. He quotes Master Cheng: Kongzi's Way is bright as the sun and stars, yet he still feared his disciples could not fully see it, and so said 'I would like to have no words'; a Yan Hui would have understood in silence; the rest could not help doubting and asking, hence 'what shall we hand on'; and then 'what words has Heaven? The four seasons move on, the hundred things are born' — that can be called perfectly plain. Zhu Xi adds that this throws light on the 'nothing hidden' of the earlier book (7.23), and the learner should consider them together. He Yan has no comment on these words.

sentences.t:
孺悲欲見孔子，
孔子辭以疾。
將命者出戸，
取瑟而歌，使之聞之。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Ru Bei wanted an audience with Kongzi, and Kongzi sent word that he was ill. But no sooner was the messenger out of the door than he took down his zither and sang, so that the man would hear.
sentences.n: 孺悲 Ru Bei: Zhu Xi: a man of Lu who had once studied the mourning rites for an officer (士喪禮) with Kongzi; at this time he must have done something to give offence, so Kongzi declined on grounds of illness, and then let him know it was not illness, to warn and teach him (故辭以疾而又使知其非疾以警教之也). 見 jiàn 'to see', to call on. 辭以疾 'declined by reason of illness'. 將命者 'the one carrying the message', who passed words between host and guest (as 14.47); 將 is jiāng. 戸 is the edition's form of 戶 'door'. 瑟 the zither (11.14). 使之聞之 'made him hear it': the second 之 is the song; the first, for Zhu Xi, is Ru Bei himself. He quotes Master Cheng: this is what Mencius calls the teaching that disdains to teach, by which one teaches more deeply (此孟子所謂不屑之教誨所以深教之也). He Yan's own comment takes the hearer to be the messenger: Ru Bei was a man of Lu; Kongzi did not wish to see him and declined on grounds of illness; and because the messenger would not know the reason, he sang, to bring the messenger to understand — and through him to make Ru Bei think. Variant: He Yan's text reads 孔子辭之以疾 'Kongzi declined him on the grounds of illness', with 之.

sentences.t:
宰我問：「
三年之喪，期已久矣。」

morph.gloss: a steward, the chief officer of a noble house

sentences.l:
Zai Wo asked:
“Three years' mourning — a full year is long already.”
sentences.i: Zai Wo put a question: “Mourning for three years — a single year is already a long time.”
sentences.n: 宰我 Zai Wo (3.21), whose personal name 予 Yu the Master uses below. 三年之喪 'the three years' mourning', for a parent; 喪 is sāng 'mourning'. 期 is jī 'a full year' (Zhu Xi: 期音基下同…期周年也; as 13.10 期月). 已 'already'; 久 'long'. Zai Wo's words run on past Zhu Xi's comments; the next two units are left unquoted.

sentences.t:
君子三年不為禮，
禮必壞；
三年不為樂，
樂必崩。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: If a gentleman leaves off the rites for three years, the rites are bound to fall into disrepair; if he leaves off music for three years, music is bound to fall apart.
sentences.n: Still Zai Wo, unquoted. 為 wéi 'to do, to practise'; 樂 yuè 'music'. 壞 huài 'to go to ruin'; 崩 'to collapse' (as 16.1). Zhu Xi: he fears that during the mourning they will not be practised, and so will collapse and go to ruin (恐居喪不習而崩壞也).

sentences.t:
舊榖既没，
新榖既升，
鑚燧改火，
期可已矣。
sentences.l:
The old grain is already used up,
the new grain already come up,
the fire-wood drilled and the fire changed —
a full year, and it can stop.
sentences.i: By then the old grain is eaten and the new grain is in, and the fire has been drilled anew from each season's wood. After one year the mourning could well come to an end.
sentences.n: Still Zai Wo, unquoted. 榖 gǔ is the edition's form of 穀 'grain'; 没 the edition's form of 沒, 'gone, used up' (Zhu Xi: 没盡也); 升 'to come up' (升登也), the new crop has come in. 鑚 zuān 'to drill' (Zhu Xi: 祖官反); 燧 suì: the wood fire is drilled from (燧取火之木也). 改火 'change the fire': Zhu Xi: in spring fire is taken from elm and willow, in summer from jujube and apricot, in late summer from mulberry and zhe (柘), in autumn from the zuo and you trees (柞楢), in winter from the huai and tan (槐檀) — and in one year it too comes full round. 期 jī 'a full year' (as 42). 已 'to stop' (已止也). Zhu Xi: in a full year Heaven's course makes one round and the things of the seasons have all changed, so (Zai Wo argues) mourning can stop there. He quotes Yin Tun: the talk of shortened mourning is something even the lowest fool would be ashamed to utter; Zai Wo studied at the sage's own gate and still asked it — he had a doubt in his heart and did not dare force himself past it (有所疑於心而不敢强焉爾). Ma Rong in He Yan gives the same round of woods from the Monthly Ordinances in the Zhou documents (周書月令有更火): because each season drills fire from a different wood, it is called changing the fire.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
食夫稻，
衣夫錦，
於女安乎？」
曰：「安。」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Eating that rice,
wearing that brocade —
would you be at ease?”
He said: “At ease.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “And you would eat your fine rice and wear your brocade, and feel easy about it?” “I would,” said Zai Wo.
sentences.n: 食 shí 'to eat'; 衣 yì 'to wear' (Zhu Xi: 衣去聲); 夫 fú 'that' (夫音扶下同); 稻 dào 'rice', 錦 jǐn 'brocade' — the best food and the finest dress. 於女安乎 'to you, at ease?' — 女 rǔ 'you' (女音汝下同). Zhu Xi: by the rites, in mourning for a parent, after the encoffining one eats gruel and wears coarse sackcloth; after the burial, coarse grain and water, and the mourning cloth is changed for finished cloth; at the first year's lesser auspicious sacrifice (小祥) one begins to eat vegetables and fruit and wears a cap of glossed silk with a pink border, but the waist-band of mourning is not put off — there is no question of eating rice or wearing brocade (無食稻衣錦之理). The Master wanted Zai Wo to search his own heart and find for himself why one cannot bear it, so he asked him this; and Zai Wo did not see it. Variants: He Yan's text reads 食夫稻也，衣夫錦也, with two 也; and it prints 曰安之 where Zhu Xi has 曰安 and begins the next unit with 女 — as printed, the 之 could end Zai Wo's answer ('at ease with it') or begin the Master's reply.

sentences.t:
女安則為之！
夫君子之居喪，
食旨不甘，
聞樂不樂，
居處不安，
故不為也。
今女安則為之！

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
If you are at ease, then do it!
Now the gentleman, dwelling in mourning,
eats fine food and does not find it sweet,
hears music and does not enjoy it,
stays at home and is not at ease,
and so he does not do it.
Now you are at ease — then do it!
sentences.i: If it sits easy with you, go ahead. When a gentleman is in mourning, the choicest food has no savour for him, music gives him no pleasure, and he cannot rest easy at home; that is why he does not do it. But if it sits easy with you, go ahead.
sentences.n: These are the Master's words, though the text gives no 子曰 here (Zhu Xi: 此夫子之言也); they follow straight on Zai Wo's 'At ease' and are left unquoted. 女 rǔ 'you'; 則 'then'; 為之 'do it' (為 wéi). 夫 fú opens a general statement. 居喪 'to dwell in mourning' (喪 sāng). 食 shí 'to eat'; 旨 zhǐ 'fine-tasting': Zhu Xi: 旨 too is 'sweet' (旨亦甘也); Kong Anguo in He Yan: 旨 is 'delicious' (旨美也); 甘 gān 'sweet, to relish'. 聞樂不樂: the first 樂 is yuè 'music', the second lè 'to enjoy' (Zhu Xi: 樂上如字下音洛). 居處 'staying in one's quarters', 處 chǔ. Zhu Xi: the first 'if you are at ease, do it' are words that cut him off; then the Master brings out the first stirrings of not being able to bear it, to warn him for not seeing, and says 'if you are at ease, do it' again to rebuke him deeply. Kong Anguo in He Yan: he rebukes him for lacking humaneness toward his parents, and so says it twice.

sentences.t:
宰我出。
子曰：「
予之不仁也！
子生三年，然後免於父母之懷。
夫三年之喪，天下之通喪也。
予也有三年之愛於其父母乎？」

morph.gloss: a steward, the chief officer of a noble house

sentences.l:
Zai Wo went out.
The Master said:
“How lacking in humaneness Yu is!
A child is born, and only after three years does it leave the arms of father and mother.
Now three years' mourning is the mourning common to all the world.
Has Yu three years of love for his father and mother?”
sentences.i: When Zai Wo had gone out, the Master said: “How little humaneness there is in Yu! A child is three years old before it leaves its parents' arms. Three years' mourning is kept by everyone, from the highest to the lowest. Has Yu not even three years' love to give his parents?”
sentences.n: 予 here is yǔ, Zai Wo's personal name (as 5.9), the Master speaking of him after he has left — not the pronoun yú 'I'. 予之不仁也 'Yu's lack of humaneness!': 之 makes it one phrase, and the sentence is an exclamation. 子生三年，然後免 'a child is born, three years, and only then gets free'; 然後 'only after that'; 懷 'the arms, the bosom' (Zhu Xi: 懷抱也; Ma Rong in He Yan: until it is three, a child is carried in its parents' arms). 夫 fú opens the general statement. 通喪 'a mourning common to all' (通 tōng): Kong Anguo in He Yan: from the Son of Heaven down to the common people (自天子達於庶人). The last line can be taken two ways, as 於 is 'for' or 'from': 'has Yu three years of love for his parents?' — which suits Zhu Xi's gloss below — or 'Yu had three years of love from his parents, surely?' Zhu Xi: when Zai Wo had gone out, the Master feared he would really think it could be borne and go and do it, so he probed to the root and rebuked him: it is because he is not humane that his love for his parents is this thin (言由其不仁故愛親之薄如此也); and he told why the gentleman cannot bear it with his parents and mourning must be three years, so that, hearing of it, Zai Wo might look into himself and in the end find his true heart. He quotes Fan Zuyu: though mourning stops at three years, a worthy man's feeling has no end; only because the sage set the measure at the mean and one dare not go past it, one bows down to it — it is not that three years' mourning is enough to repay one's parents; 'three years before leaving the parents' arms' was said only to rebuke Zai Wo's want of gratitude (無恩), wishing him to stretch up and reach it. Kong Anguo in He Yan: a son's wish to repay his parents' kindness is as boundless as high Heaven (昊天罔極, the words of an ode), and yet Yu has (only) three years' love. Variant: He Yan's text reads 宰我出曰, without 子 — probably a slip, since the words that follow can only be the Master's.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
飽食終日，
無所用心，
難矣哉！
不有博奕者乎？
為之，猶賢乎已。」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Eating one's fill all day long,
with nothing to use the mind on —
hard indeed!
Are there not bo and weiqi?
Playing them is still better than stopping.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “To eat your fill from morning to night and give your mind to nothing — that is a hard case! Aren't there games of bo and of weiqi? Even playing those beats letting the mind lie fallow.”
sentences.n: 飽食 'to eat one's fill' (食 shí); 終日 'all day long'. 無所用心 'having nothing on which to use the mind': 所 + verb, 'that on which'. 難矣哉 'hard indeed!' — the Master leaves unsaid what is hard. 不有…乎 'are there not…?'. 博 bó: Zhu Xi: a board game (博局戲也); 奕 yì: weiqi, the game of surrounding (奕圍棊也). 賢乎已 'better than stopping': 賢 'better', 乎 'than' (= 於), 已 'to stop', doing nothing (Zhu Xi: 已止也). Zhu Xi quotes Mr Li (李氏): the sage is not teaching people to play bo and weiqi; he is only saying in the strongest terms that having nothing to use the mind on will not do (所以甚言無所用心之不可爾). He Yan's comment explains the games as better because, with nothing to hold to, idle pleasure breeds dissolute desires — the wording of the comment (為其無所據樂善生淫慾) is not clear in the transcription.

sentences.t:
子路曰：「君子尚勇乎？」
子曰：「
君子義以為上。
君子有勇而無義為亂，
小人有勇而無義為盜。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu said: “Does the gentleman prize courage?”
The Master said:
“The gentleman takes what is right as highest.
A gentleman with courage but without what is right makes disorder;
a small man with courage but without what is right turns robber.”
sentences.i: Zilu said: “Does the gentleman set great store by courage?” The Master said: “The gentleman puts what is right above all else. A gentleman who has courage and no sense of what is right will stir up rebellion; a small man who has courage and no sense of what is right will take to robbery.”
sentences.n: 尚 'to prize': Zhu Xi: 尚 is to put it highest (尚上之也). 義以為上 is 以義為上 'takes what is right as highest', with the object brought forward, as in 15.17 義以為質; 為 wéi 'to take as', and below 'to make, to become'. Zhu Xi: the gentleman who makes rebellion and the small man who turns robber are both named by rank (皆以位而言者也) — the man in high place and the commoner, not the men of good and bad character. He quotes Yin Tun: if one takes what is right as highest, one's courage is great indeed; Zilu loved courage (5.6), so the Master said this to correct his fault; and Hu Yin: he suspects this was a question and answer from when Zilu first met Kongzi. He Yan has no comment. Variant: Ruan Yuan's text reads 君子義之為上, with 之 for 以 marking the object put first; the sense is the same.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「君子亦有惡乎？」
子曰：「
有惡：
惡稱人之惡者，
惡居下流而訕上者，
惡勇而無禮者，
惡果敢而窒者。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zigong said: “Are there things the gentleman hates as well?” The Master said: “There are. He hates those who broadcast other people's faults. He hates those in low places who rail at those above them. He hates the brave who have no regard for the rites, and the bold and decisive whose minds are shut.”
sentences.n: 惡 is wù 'to hate' throughout (Zhu Xi: 惡去聲下同), except in 稱人之惡, where it is è 'the bad (in others)' (唯惡者之惡如字). 亦 'too': may the gentleman, too, hate? 稱 chēng 'to speak of, to make known'. 下流 'the lower stream', a low place; 訕 shàn (Zhu Xi: 所諌反) 'to slander': Zhu Xi and Kong Anguo in He Yan, 訕謗毁也. 勇而無禮 'brave but without the rites', as 8.2. 果敢 'resolute and daring' (果 as 6.6); 窒 zhì 'blocked': Zhu Xi, not getting through (窒不通也); Ma Rong in He Yan, stopped up (窒塞也). Each clause ends in 者 'the ones who…'. Zhu Xi: proclaiming others' bad points shows no humane generosity; slandering those above from below shows no wholehearted respect; brave without the rites, one makes disorder; resolute but blocked, one acts recklessly — so the Master hated them. Bao Xian in He Yan: one who likes to tell of others' bad points is himself bad for it (好稱說人悪所以為悪也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 子貢問曰, adding 問.

sentences.t:
曰：「賜也亦有惡乎？」「
惡徼以為知者，
惡不孫以為勇者，
惡訐以為直者。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “And you, Ci — are there things you hate?” “I hate those who think prying makes them wise, those who think it brave to forget their place, and those who think laying bare other people's secrets makes them upright.”
sentences.n: The 曰 is the Master's: he turns the question back, calling Zigong by his personal name 賜 Ci (1.15); and from 惡徼 on, Zhu Xi says, the words are Zigong's (惡徼以下子貢之言也), so his reply is set as a second quotation with no verb of saying. 以為 'to take (it) as'. 徼 jiāo (Zhu Xi: 古堯反, a level tone): Zhu Xi, 'to spy, to pry' (伺察也); Kong Anguo in He Yan reads it as 抄 'to lift': taking others' ideas as one's own (抄人之意以為巳有). 知 zhì 'wise, wisdom' and 孫 xùn 'humble' (= 遜): Zhu Xi, 知孫並去聲. 訐 jié (居謁反): Zhu Xi and Bao Xian in He Yan, attacking and laying bare others' private affairs (攻發人之隂私). 直 'straight', as 13.18. Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: the humane man loves all, so it might seem the gentleman has no hates; Zigong had this thought, so he asked, to test whether it was right; and Hou Zhongliang: such are the hates of sages and worthies — what is meant by 'only the humane can hate people' (唯仁者能惡人; 4.3). Variant: He Yan's text reads 賜也亦有惡也, with 也 for 乎, which can be read as Zigong's own words: 'I, Ci, have hates too.'

sentences.t:
子曰：「
唯女子與小人為難養也：
近之則不孫，
逺之則怨。」

morph.gloss: women (here, the women who serve in a household)

sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Only women and servants are hard to keep:
bring them near, and they are not humble;
hold them far off, and they bear a grudge.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “In a household none are so hard to look after as the women and the servants. Let them close and they forget their place; hold them off and they nurse grievances.”
sentences.n: 唯 wéi 'only, it is just… that'. 女子 nǚ zǐ 'women' — 女 here is nǚ 'woman', not rǔ 'you'. 與 yǔ 'and'. 小人 here is not the morally small man set against the gentleman: Zhu Xi: this 小人 too means servants and underlings (此小人亦謂僕𨽻下人也). He does not gloss 女子, but his next words speak of the gentleman's dealings with his 臣妾, his menservants and women servants, which places both words inside the household: in his reading the line is about the women who serve in it and the menservants, not about women as such. 為 wéi 'to be'; 難 nán 'hard'; 養 yǎng 'to keep, to provide for', as a master keeps his household. 近 jìn 'to bring near', 逺 'to keep far off' (Zhu Xi: 近孫逺並去聲 — he reads the verb 逺 yuàn, as at 15.10, a reading modern practice does not keep; we print yuǎn); 孫 xùn 'humble' (= 遜, as 7.35); 怨 'to resent, bear a grudge'. Zhu Xi: if the gentleman oversees his servants with gravity and keeps them with kindness (莊以涖之慈以畜之), he will be free of both troubles. He Yan has no comment on the chapter.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
年四十而見惡焉，
其終也已。」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“At forty years, and still disliked —
he ends there, and that is all.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If a man is forty and people still dislike him, he will go no further.”
sentences.n: 年四十 'in years, forty' — the age of being no longer perplexed (2.4); Zhu Xi: forty is the time when virtue is made (四十成徳之時). 見 jiàn before a verb makes it passive: 見惡 'is disliked' (惡 wù; Zhu Xi: 惡去聲). 焉 yān 'by them, among others'. 其終也已 'he ends, and that is all'. Zhu Xi: to be disliked by others at the time when virtue should be made means he will stop there and go no further; it urges people to turn to the good and correct their faults while there is time (勉人及時遷善改過也). He quotes Su Shi: this too was said with someone in view; who, we cannot know (此亦有為而言不知其為誰也). Zheng Xuan in He Yan: at the age of not being perplexed and still disliked by people, he will never have good conduct (终無善行也). Compare 9.22, 'at forty or fifty, if nothing is heard of them'.
